113.title: The thousandth lotus
113.hook: Vishnu, one lotus short, offers his own eye; why the flower on the shrine stands for the one who offers it
113.carry: the flower stands for your heart
113.howItsDone: Many Hindus place fresh flowers at the home shrine each morning as an offering of devotion (bhakti), taking down the previous day's, usually not offering a fallen flower or smelling one meant for the shrine, and often choosing flowers or leaves dear to a particular deity, such as hibiscus for Ganesha, bilva for Shiva and tulsi for Vishnu or Krishna.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-THIRTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, deepa, the lamp. Your line was the lamp's light is greeted as god. Today, the thing on the plate that won't last the day, and a god who ran out of them.
screen: `DEEPA — THE LAMP'S LIGHT IS GREETED AS GOD.`

segments.voice: The gods were losing to the demons, and Vishnu went to Shiva's mountain to ask for help. He didn't come empty-handed. He brought a thousand lotuses, one for each of Shiva's thousand names, and began: a name, a flower. A name, a flower. Shiva watched, and decided to test him. Quietly, he hid one lotus. Nine hundred and ninety-nine names in, Vishnu reached into the basket, and it was empty. He didn't stop the prayer. He didn't send anyone to find another flower. People call Vishnu lotus-eyed. So he got ready to offer his own eye.
screen: `A THOUSAND NAMES, A THOUSAND LOTUSES.` → `SHIVA HIDES ONE.` → `THE BASKET IS EMPTY.` → `VISHNU OFFERS HIS OWN EYE.`

segments.voice: Shiva stopped him, deeply moved, and gave Vishnu the shining discus he carries ever since, the Sudarshana. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it. Look at what the story says a flower is. When the basket ran out, Vishnu didn't see a missing decoration. He saw a gap only he could fill, because the flower had been standing in for him the whole time. That's the heart of bhakti, devotion, the path of love: in puja, the flower is a stand-in for the one who offers it. Krishna says the same thing another way: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with love, and I accept it. The price doesn't matter. The heart does. So a shrine flower comes with small habits. It's picked fresh for the morning, and yesterday's is taken down. One that fell on the floor is usually not offered. It's often left unsmelled, because the first enjoyment isn't the giver's. Different forms of God have favorites: red hibiscus for Ganesha and the Goddess, bilva leaves for Shiva, tulsi for Vishnu and Krishna. And by evening it droops, so tomorrow you bring a new one, the way you bring yourself again. Many teachers read it simply: the flower on the plate is really you. So a silk flower can sit there all year, and it's pretty. It just can't stand in for anyone.
screen: `SHIVA GIVES THE SUDARSHANA.` · `BHAKTI: THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOU.` · `PICKED FRESH, LEFT UNSMELLED.` · `A NEW ONE TOMORROW, LIKE YOU.`

segments.voice: Find a flower or a leaf near you, or picture one, and look at it closely: the color, the veins, the edge that won't look like this tomorrow. Set it down somewhere that matters to you, your corner, a windowsill, beside a photo of someone you love. If you pray, offer it with a name you honor, Om namah shivaya, or Krishna's name, and let it carry you with it. If you don't pray, name one thing you're bringing with it today, and sit with it.
Pushpa. The flower: picked fresh, left unsmelled, and offered in your place, the way Vishnu's lotuses were.
screen: `PUSHPA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the flower stands for your heart. Vishnu was ready to give himself when the flowers ran out. That's day one hundred thirteen.

114.title: The name he called
114.hook: Ajamila, dying and afraid, calls his son Narayana and Vishnu's messengers come; why puja begins with a call, and the bell sounds it
114.carry: the bell is a call: come
114.howItsDone: Many Hindus ring a small hand bell at the start of puja as part of inviting the deity (avahana), often saying a short traditional verse, ring it again during arti, and ring the large bell at a temple's entrance as they walk in. Many hand bells carry a figure on the handle, often Garuda for Vishnu's devotees or Nandi for Shiva's.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FOURTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, pushpa, and Vishnu ready to give his own eye. Your line was the flower stands for your heart. Today, the small thing with a handle, and a man who called a name.
screen: `PUSHPA — THE FLOWER STANDS FOR YOUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Ajamila started out as a good young man who kept every rule. Then he fell for the wrong life, left his wife, and lived for decades by cheating and stealing. He had ten children, and he adored the youngest, a little boy named Narayana, one of Vishnu's names. At eighty-eight, Ajamila lay dying, and he saw them coming: three terrifying messengers of Death, ropes in their hands. He panicked, and did what a frightened father does. He shouted for his little boy, playing outside. Narayana! He wasn't praying. He was just calling his son.
screen: `A GOOD MAN WHO WENT WRONG.` → `HIS YOUNGEST SON: NARAYANA.` → `DEATH'S MESSENGERS ARRIVE.` → `HE CALLS THE NAME.`

segments.voice: But the name he called was God's. And in the Bhagavata Purana, the moment it leaves his mouth, Vishnu's own messengers appear and stop Death's messengers cold. They argue it out, and Vishnu's side wins: a name of God, called even by accident, even half-meant, is heard. Ajamila is released, and he spends the rest of his life in prayer. Some families say that's one reason so many Hindu children carry God's names: every time you call them, you've called God too. Now, the bell. Its Sanskrit name is ghanta. Every puja begins with a call, called avahana: inviting God to come. And the bell is the sound of that call. Many families say a short traditional verse as they ring it, asking the gods to come and anything in the way to go. So the bell isn't an alarm clock for a sleepy God. It's a call, made by someone who trusts, like the story does, that calling is enough to be heard. That's why it rings at the very start of puja, again through arti, and why people ring the big bell at a temple door as they walk in. On top of many hand bells sits a little figure: Garuda, the eagle who carries Vishnu, or Nandi, Shiva's bull. Many teachers add a second reading: the bell calls you too. By the time its long ring fades, you're here.
screen: `VISHNU'S MESSENGERS STOP DEATH'S.` · `GHANTA: PUJA BEGINS WITH A CALL.` · `NOT AN ALARM CLOCK. A CALL.` · `THE BELL CALLS YOU TOO.`

segments.voice: Strike a bell once, gently, or a glass with a spoon, or just imagine the sound. If you pray, let the ring be your call, and say one name you honor, Narayana, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, quietly, once. Then don't move. Follow the sound as it thins out, until you can't tell whether you still hear it. When it's gone, notice where you are. You were called too.
Ghanta. The bell: rung at the start of puja to call God in, the sound of a call that, the story says, is always heard.
screen: `GHANTA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the bell is a call: come. Ajamila only called his son's name, and it was enough. Day one hundred fourteen, done.

115.title: The river that came down
115.hook: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga down from heaven and Shiva catches her in his hair; why a drop of Ganga water purifies the puja cup
115.carry: the ganga came down to purify
115.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep a small vessel of Ganga water (Ganga jal) at home, add a drop to the puja water, sprinkle it to purify, and give a little to the dying; in puja, water is offered to the deity as to an honored guest, sipped by the worshipper to begin clean, and received back afterward as a blessing.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-FIFTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, ghanta, the bell, and a man who called a name. Your line was the bell is a call: come. Today, the plainest thing on the shelf, and the river behind it.
screen: `GHANTA — THE BELL IS A CALL: COME.`

segments.voice: King Sagara had sixty thousand sons, and he sent them all to find a lost sacred horse. They dug through the earth looking for it, and found it grazing beside a sage deep in meditation, Kapila. They called him a thief and rushed at him. He turned on them, and they were burned to ash. For generations their ashes lay there, and nothing could free them, except, the wise said, the Ganga, the river of heaven, if she would come down to earth. Kings tried and failed. Then their great-great-grandson, Bhagiratha, gave up his throne and prayed for years, until the river agreed. One problem: a river falling from heaven would smash the earth.
screen: `SIXTY THOUSAND SONS.` → `BURNED TO ASH BY A SAGE.` → `ONLY THE GANGA CAN FREE THEM.` → `BHAGIRATHA PRAYS FOR YEARS.`

segments.voice: So Shiva stood beneath her and caught the whole river in his matted hair, and let her out gently, in streams. Bhagiratha drove ahead in his chariot, and the Ganga followed him all the way to the ashes. Her water touched them, and Sagara's sons were freed and rose to heaven. That's the Ramayana's telling, and it's why images of Shiva show a little river spilling from his hair. Even now, in Hindi, a huge effort is called Bhagiratha's effort. Here's the teaching. For Hindus, the Ganga isn't just a river. She's Ganga Ma, a goddess and a mother, and her water purifies. That's why so many Hindu homes keep a small bottle of Ganga water, Ganga jal, often brought back from a pilgrimage. A drop goes into the puja cup. It's sprinkled to make a place or a person ready. A little is given to someone who is dying, and ashes are carried to the river, the way Sagara's sons were freed. And the small cup on your shelf echoes it every morning. Before puja, many people sip a little water from the palm, to begin clean. Water is offered to wash God's feet and hands, like a guest's. Then it comes back to the family, a few drops in the palm, as a blessing. The plainest thing on the shelf carries the biggest river.
screen: `SHIVA CATCHES THE RIVER IN HIS HAIR.` · `GANGA MA: HER WATER PURIFIES.` · `GANGA JAL, KEPT AT HOME.` · `THE SMALL CUP ON YOUR SHELF.`

segments.voice: With a small cup of water, or at a sink, wash your hands slowly, as if you were about to greet someone you honor. Then pour a few drops somewhere as a gift: a houseplant, the soil outside, the cup in your corner. If you pray, you can say Ganga's name, or a name you honor, as the water goes. Then take one small sip and notice it: washed, given, received, the way the river came down.
The water. In puja it washes, it's offered, and it comes back as blessing; and a drop of the Ganga, the river that came down, makes it holy.
screen: `THE WATER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Ganga came down to purify. Shiva caught her so she wouldn't break the world. One hundred fifteen days now.

116.title: One leaf in the pot
116.hook: Krishna eats one leaf from Draupadi's empty pot and ten thousand hungry sages feel full; why food goes to God first and comes back as prasad
116.carry: when god is fed, everyone is fed
116.tomorrow: The paste meant for a king
116.howItsDone: Many Hindus place a small portion of food, often a sweet or fruit, before the image at the home shrine as naivedya, wait a few moments, and then receive it back as prasad, grace, sharing it with everyone in the house and any guests.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-SIXTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the water, and the river Shiva caught in his hair. Your line was the Ganga came down to purify. Today, the sweet on the plate, and an empty pot.
screen: `THE WATER — THE GANGA CAME DOWN TO PURIFY.`

segments.voice: The Pandavas are living in exile in the forest, and they have one treasure: a pot from the Sun god that gives food every day, until Draupadi has eaten. Then it's empty till morning. Their cousin Duryodhana knows this. So he sends them a guest: the sage Durvasa, famous for his temper, with ten thousand disciples, timed to arrive just after Draupadi has finished her meal. Durvasa says: we'll bathe in the river, then we eat. Draupadi looks at the empty pot. If she can't feed them, the curse will be terrible. So she closes her eyes and calls Krishna.
screen: `A POT THAT FEEDS THEM DAILY.` → `UNTIL DRAUPADI EATS.` → `TEN THOUSAND HUNGRY GUESTS.` → `SHE CALLS KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Krishna appears, and the first thing he says is: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat. Draupadi almost cries: there's nothing, that's the whole problem. Bring the pot, he says. Stuck to the rim is one tiny leaf of cooked greens. Krishna eats it, and says: may the one who is the soul of the whole world be satisfied. Down at the river, ten thousand sages suddenly feel completely full. They're too embarrassed to come back, and they slip away. That's how the Mahabharata tells it. Here's the teaching. Krishna's line names it: God is the soul in every being, so feeding God is never feeding just one. An old Hindu picture puts it simply: water the root of a tree, and every branch is fed. That's naivedya, today's word: food offered to God before anyone eats. The cook often doesn't taste it while cooking, because the first taste isn't theirs. A little goes before the image on a clean plate, sometimes with a tulsi leaf on top, and sits for a few moments. Then the plate comes back, and it isn't just food anymore. It's prasad, grace, and it's shared with everyone: the family, the guest at the door, the neighbor. People take it in the right hand, often with a small bow, and try not to refuse it. Feed God first, and the food comes back for all. That's why the laddus wait.
screen: `ONE LEAF ON THE RIM.` · `TEN THOUSAND SAGES FEEL FULL.` · `NAIVEDYA: GOD EATS FIRST.` · `PRASAD: IT COMES BACK FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Set something small to eat in front of you, a piece of fruit, a square of chocolate, a few raisins, and pause before you eat it. If you pray, offer it first, to Krishna or a name you honor, and wait a few breaths before you take it back as prasad. If you don't pray, hold it as a gift you didn't make by yourself: the sun, the farmer, the driver. Then break it in two if you can, put half aside for someone else, and eat your half slowly.
Naivedya. Food offered to God before anyone eats, which comes back as prasad for everyone, like one leaf that fed ten thousand.

segments.voice: Krishna is a teenager, walking into the city of Mathura for the first time, the city of the cruel king Kamsa. On the street he meets a young woman bent nearly double, her back badly curved. People call her Kubja, the hunchback. She's carrying a dish of fragrant sandalwood paste, the best in the city, for the king himself. Krishna smiles and asks: who's that for? Could we have some? She looks up at him. It's the king's paste, and she is the king's servant. She gives it anyway, generously, with her own hands, to Krishna and his brother.
screen: `A STREET IN MATHURA.` → `A WOMAN BENT DOUBLE.` → `SANDAL PASTE FOR THE KING.` → `SHE GIVES IT TO KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: Krishna is delighted. He steps on her toes gently, puts two fingers under her chin, and lifts, and her back straightens. She stands tall for the first time in her life. That's how the Bhagavata Purana tells it. Look at what she did. She served God with what was in her hands, the most precious thing she had. That's puja. Its offerings are called upacharas, services, the way you'd serve an honored guest. Old manuals give a short five-part form: fragrance, flower, incense, lamp and food. Fragrance comes first, often sandal paste, Kubja's gift, touched to the image. This week you've learned the rest, and on a school morning it can all fit in four minutes. Ring the bell: you're calling God in. Light the lamp. Offer a fresh flower, which stands for your heart. A few drops of water. Some sandal paste or incense if you have it. Something sweet, which comes back as prasad. Then a name or a mantra said quietly, and pranam, the bow. Families do it in different orders, and some mornings it's only a lamp and a bow. That counts too. Notice that nobody does it for you. No priest is needed at a home shrine. Your own hands do the serving, the way Kubja's did. And many teachers read her straightened back simply: whoever serves God isn't left the same.
screen: `KRISHNA STRAIGHTENS HER BACK.` · `UPACHARA: FIVE SERVICES.` · `BELL, LAMP, FLOWER, WATER, SWEET, BOW.` · `YOUR OWN HANDS, NO PRIEST.`

segments.voice: However small your corner is, even if it's only in your mind, go through it once with your own hands. Ring a bell or tap a glass. Light the lamp, or picture it. Set down a flower or a leaf, a few drops of water and a small piece of something sweet. If you pray, quietly say your mantra or a name you honor a few times. Then put your hands together, bow, and sit for the rest of the time.
Morning puja. The home shrine, put together: bell, lamp, flower, water, sweet, a name and a bow, served with your own hands before the day begins.

118.title: The demons at dawn
118.hook: demons attack the sun at every twilight and the prayers' water drives them back; why Hindus pray at the junctions of the day
118.howItsDone: Traditionally, sandhyavandana, a prayer centered on the Gayatri mantra with water offered toward the sun (arghya), is said at dawn, noon and dusk, especially by those who wear the sacred thread; many other Hindus pour water toward the morning sun or light a lamp at dusk, and the household pauses as it's lit.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-EIGHTEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, morning puja, and Kubja's sandal paste. Your line was puja is serving God with your own hands. A new week starts today, the week of sunset and arti, and it opens with a question: when?
screen: `MORNING PUJA — PUJA IS SERVING GOD WITH YOUR OWN HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's an old story about every sunrise you've ever seen. At the edges of the day, a horde of demons called the Mandehas rise up and rush at the sun, trying to swallow it. They're under a curse: they die each day and come back each night, so the fight never ends. Every dawn, every dusk, they attack again. And what drives them back? Not armies. Not the other gods. People at prayer, standing at a riverbank, throwing a little water toward the sun. In the telling, that water, made holy by the prayer, strikes the demons like thunderbolts. And the sun climbs.
screen: `DEMONS RUSH AT THE SUN.` → `EVERY DAWN, EVERY DUSK.` → `PEOPLE AT THE RIVER, THROWING WATER.` → `THE SUN CLIMBS.`

segments.voice: That's how the Vishnu Purana tells it, and the same story is in older Vedic texts. Notice when the fight happens: not at midday, not at midnight. At the edges. Today's word is sandhya. It comes from a word for joining, the place where two things meet. So sandhya means twilight, and more: the joints of the day. Tradition names three. Dawn, where night meets day. Noon, where morning turns. Dusk, where day meets night. These are the hours Hindus set aside for prayer. The old rite for them is sandhyavandana, honoring the junctions, and at its heart is the Gayatri, the prayer to the light from day one hundred eight, said while offering water to the sun. That's the arghya from the story. It's traditionally kept by those who wear the sacred thread; many other Hindus keep a simpler form: water poured toward the morning sun, or the evening lamp lit at dusk while the house pauses. Why the edges? Many teachers say a junction belongs to neither side, so it's a door in the ordinary, and a door can be guarded. They read the demons as the darkness that tries to slip in when one part of the day hands over to the next. That's the teaching: Hindus tie prayer to the turning of the day itself, and they stand at the door when it turns.
screen: `SANDHYA — A JOINING.` · `DAWN, NOON, DUSK.` · `SANDHYAVANDANA: THE GAYATRI AND WATER TO THE SUN.` · `A JUNCTION IS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: If it's near dawn or dusk, find a window or step outside; if it isn't, remember the last sunrise or sunset you really watched. Look at the light and notice it changing. If you pray, this is one of the hours tradition sets aside: pour a little water toward the light, or just lift your hands, and say the Gayatri if you know it, or a name you honor, once. If you don't pray, simply stand at the edge of the day and notice it turn.
Sandhya. A joining: the twilight, and the three junctions of the day, dawn, noon and dusk, when the prayers go up and the sun climbs.
screen: `SANDHYA — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: pray where the day joins. That's where the old story says the light needs you. One hundred eighteen days in.

119.title: Narada's monkey face
119.hook: proud Narada asks for Vishnu's handsome face and gets a monkey's; why the arti flame burns camphor, and the ego with it
119.howItsDone: At home, many Hindus perform arti at dusk (and often at dawn) by circling a small ghee lamp or burning camphor clockwise before the image while a bell is rung and an arti song is sung; camphor, which burns away completely, is often explained as an image of offering up the ego.

screen: `DAY ONE-HUNDRED-NINETEEN.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhya, and the demons at dawn. Your line was pray where the day joins. Tonight, at dusk, the arti flame, and a sage who got far too pleased with himself.
screen: `SANDHYA — PRAY WHERE THE DAY JOINS.`

segments.voice: Narada, the wandering sage with the veena, once sat in such deep meditation that Kama, the god of desire, was sent to distract him, and failed. Narada was thrilled. I've beaten desire, he thought. Me. He told Shiva, who said kindly: wonderful, but don't go telling Vishnu. He told Vishnu. So Vishnu let him wander into a beautiful city where a princess was choosing a husband. Narada fell for her on the spot and begged Vishnu: give me your face, so she'll pick me. Vishnu said: I'll do what's best for you. Narada swept into the hall, sure he looked like Vishnu. He had the face of a monkey.
screen: `DESIRE CAN'T TOUCH HIM.` → `HE TELLS EVERYONE.` → `GIVE ME YOUR FACE.` → `HE GETS A MONKEY'S.`

segments.voice: The princess chose Vishnu. Narada caught his reflection in water, and was furious, until the whole illusion faded and he saw what had happened. He'd been so full of I, I did it, that he couldn't see. And he never forgot it. That's how the Shiva Purana tells it, and in the old pun, the word Narada asked for, hari, means both Vishnu and monkey. Here's the teaching. Hinduism calls that I-did-it voice ahamkara, the ego: literally, the I-maker. Many teachers say it's the main thing that stands between a person and God, because it takes credit for what was never only ours. And this is where arti comes in. At dusk, in many homes, someone holds a small plate with a lamp, or a piece of camphor, and circles the flame clockwise before the image while a bell rings and the family sings. Camphor is today's word. It catches fast, burns bright, and leaves no ash behind. Not a trace. Many teachers point to that: offer yourself like camphor, burn bright for God, and leave no ego behind. So when the flame goes round, notice who it's for. Not the person holding the plate, even on their first time, even if they're proud. The light goes to God. Narada learned that with a monkey's face. The camphor teaches it every evening.
screen: `NARADA SEES HIS REFLECTION.` · `AHAMKARA: THE I-MAKER.` · `CAMPHOR BURNS AND LEAVES NO ASH.` · `THE LIGHT GOES TO GOD.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle or small lamp and it's safe, light it and hold it steady on a plate in your right hand; if not, use your open hand, or just your eyes. Before an image, a photo or a window, make a few slow circles clockwise. If you pray, say a name you honor as the light goes round. Then think of one thing you're proud of this week, and offer the credit with the light. Set it down and sit with the flame.
Camphor: the arti flame that burns bright and leaves no ash, offered to God, with the ego going up along with it.
screen: `CAMPHOR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: burn the ego like camphor. Narada asked for Vishnu's face, and got a monkey's. That's day one hundred nineteen.

screen: `BURN THE EGO LIKE CAMPHOR.` → `DAY 119 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: OM JAI JAGADISH HARE.`
